summary: Mathematical principles of linear regression, parameter estimation via Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), and numerical optimization with Gradient Descent variants.
learning_objectives: Derive the Mean Squared Error (MSE) objective function.
Formulate Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) closed-form normal equations.
Understand batch, stochastic, and mini-batch gradient descent update rules.

topic_title: Introduction to Computer Networks & Network Core
summary: Foundational overview of computer networks, examining network infrastructure, edge versus core devices, packet transmission dynamics, and latency components.
learning_objectives: Understand the difference between the network edge and network core.
Explain packet switching vs circuit switching and multiplexing techniques.
Comprehend delays in packet-switched networks: processing, queuing, transmission, and propagation.

summary: Covers the modular layered architecture of computer networking protocols, protocol data units (PDU), header overhead, and end-to-end transmission dynamics.
learning_objectives: Differentiate the 5-layer Internet protocol stack from the 7-layer OSI model.
Understand protocol encapsulation and decapsulation with headers at each tier.
Analyze packet loss, buffer overflow, and throughput metrics.

topic_title: Introduction to Computer Networks, Network Core & Delay Dynamics
summary: An exhaustive, rigorous foundation in computer networking fundamentals. Explores the Internet's physical and logical topology, network edge versus core components, circuit switching vs. packet switching trade-offs, statistical multiplexing mathematics, the four components of nodal delay, and diagnostic tooling.
learning_objectives: Explain the high-level architecture of the Internet as a hierarchical 'network of networks' and the roles of ISPs, IXPs, and RFC standards.
Differentiate between the network edge (hosts, clients, servers, access networks) and the network core (mesh of routers and switches).
Compare packet switching with circuit switching, evaluating statistical multiplexing against frequency/time-division multiplexing under bursty traffic.
Derive and calculate the four nodal delay components: processing, queuing, transmission, and propagation delay, alongside the Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP).
Trace the end-to-end journey of an application request (such as visiting a website) across the protocol stack, DNS, and physical infrastructure.
Utilize fundamental diagnostic tools (ping, traceroute, iperf) to analyze network latency, hops, and throughput bottlenecks.

topic_title: Network Packets, Layered Architecture & Data Link Communication
summary: An exhaustive, rigorous deep dive into layered network design, the OSI vs. TCP/IP models, protocol encapsulation mechanics, Ethernet II framing standards, MAC address taxonomy, and Layer 2 switch forwarding and filtering algorithms.
learning_objectives: Explain the theoretical and engineering justification for layered network architecture and protocol abstraction.
Compare the 7-layer OSI reference model with the pragmatic 4/5-layer TCP/IP architectural model, categorizing Protocol Data Units (PDUs).
Trace the end-to-end mechanics of encapsulation at the sender and decapsulation at the receiver across intermediate network hops.
Dissect the byte-by-byte anatomy of an Ethernet II frame, explaining preambles, EtherType demultiplexing, minimum payload padding, and FCS CRC-32.
Contrast link-layer MAC addressing (EUI-48, OUI, U/L and I/G bits) with network-layer IP addressing and transport-layer port numbers.
Demonstrate how Layer 2 switches perform transparent bridging via the MAC learning algorithm, CAM tables, filtering, flooding, and aging.

topic_title: IPv4 Addressing, Subnetting, CIDR & Special Address Blocks
summary: An exhaustive, rigorous masterclass in IPv4 architecture. Details binary numbering, classful history, CIDR prefix mechanics, bitwise AND operations, the mathematical foundations of subnetting, VLSM engineering, RFC-reserved address spaces, ARP vs CAM table distinctions, and MTU fragmentation mechanics.
learning_objectives: Explain why logical hierarchical IP addressing is required for global routing instead of flat hardware MAC addresses.
Perform rapid, bidirectional binary-to-decimal and decimal-to-binary conversions across all 8-bit octet boundaries.
Critique legacy classful addressing (Classes A, B, C, D, E) and explain the historical drivers behind the IPv4 address exhaustion crisis.
Apply bitwise ANDing between IPv4 addresses and subnet masks to determine network IDs and route forwarding decisions.
Master the step-by-step 'Magic Number' subnetting algorithm to compute network addresses, broadcast addresses, and usable host ranges (2^H - 2).
Categorize reserved IPv4 blocks: RFC 1918 private spaces (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16), loopback (127/8), APIPA (169.254/16), and RFC 3021 /31 point-to-point links.
Distinguish between the Layer 3 Host/Router ARP Table and the Layer 2 Switch MAC (CAM) Table.
Analyze Link-Layer MTU constraints and calculate IPv4 fragmentation offsets and flags (DF, MF) using the 8-byte alignment rule.

topic_title: Advanced Subnetting, Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) & IPv6 Architecture
summary: An exhaustive, rigorous masterclass in advanced IP network engineering. Details the 5-step mathematical process to derive custom subnets from host requirements, Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) departmental hierarchies, host routing decision flows via default gateways, Network Address Translation (NAT/PAT), and the 128-bit IPv6 addressing architecture, compression algorithms, and comparative protocol mechanics.
learning_objectives: Master the 5-step requirements-to-subnet mathematical algorithm for arbitrary host and network constraints.
Implement equal-length subnet splitting and calculate network IDs, first/last usable hosts, and broadcast addresses across octet boundaries.
Apply Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) using the Golden Rule (largest subnet first) to eliminate address wastage in multi-department enterprise topologies.
Analyze default gateway decision logic: bitwise masking, local ARP broadcast vs. gateway forwarding.
Examine Network Address Translation (NAT/PAT/Masquerade) mechanics, SNAT vs DNAT port forwarding, and its impact on the end-to-end principle.
Dissect IPv6 128-bit architecture, colon-hex notation, zero-compression rules, address taxonomy (Link-Local, Multicast, Global Unicast, Loopback), and protocol differences with IPv4.

topic_title: Graph Theory in Networking - BFS, DFS, Adjacency Models & Cycle Detection
summary: An exhaustive, rigorous masterclass in graph theory fundamentals applied to computer networks. Explores graph mathematical modeling G = (V, E), sparse internet topology vs. dense matrix representations, Breadth-First Search (BFS) hop-count pathfinding and path reconstruction, Depth-First Search (DFS) topology exploration, the canonical Layer 2 cycle detection algorithm, and Spanning Tree Protocol (STP / 802.1D) broadcast storm elimination.
learning_objectives: Model complex network topologies as weighted graphs G = (V, E) with propagation delay, inverse bandwidth, and administrative link costs.
Contrast Adjacency List (O(V+E) space) and Adjacency Matrix (O(V^2) space) representations, explaining why the sparse Internet topology mandates adjacency lists.
Implement and trace Breadth-First Search (BFS) using FIFO queues to discover minimum-hop paths and reconstruct routes via parent pointers.
Analyze the fundamental architectural limitation of BFS (hop-count minimization vs. latency/bandwidth minimization) and recognize when Dijkstra is required.
Implement Depth-First Search (DFS) with recursion and explicit stacks for complete network topology discovery.
Dissect the canonical parent-pointer cycle detection algorithm and explain why Layer 2 Ethernet loops cause catastrophic broadcast storms without Spanning Tree Protocol (STP).

topic_title: Shortest Path Routing - Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford & Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)
summary: An exhaustive, rigorous masterclass in shortest path routing algorithms and graph theory fundamentals for computer networks. Covers why Dijkstra fails on negative-weight edges, the complete 8-node MinHeap Dijkstra trace, Bellman-Ford algorithm and dynamic programming edge relaxation, negative cycle detection, Minimum Spanning Trees (MST) and Prim's algorithm, and the foundational architectural differences between Distance Vector (RIP, BGP) and Link State (OSPF, IS-IS) routing protocol families.
learning_objectives: Prove why Dijkstra's greedy algorithm fails on networks with negative edge weights, identifying the exact root cause in greedy finalization.
Execute the complete 8-node MinHeap Dijkstra trace step-by-step (nodes A through H), detailing heap insertions, distance updates, and stale entry discards.
Implement the Bellman-Ford algorithm, explaining why V - 1 iterations are mathematically required and sufficient to compute all simple shortest paths.
Formulate the V-th iteration negative weight cycle detection mechanism and analyze its network equivalent (infinite routing loops / metric sinks).

Contrast Distance Vector (Bellman-Ford based: RIP, BGP) and Link State (Dijkstra based: OSPF, IS-IS) routing protocol families in terms of topology knowledge, convergence speed, bandwidth overhead, and loop vulnerability.
Dissect Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) algorithms (Prim's algorithm with priority queues) and explain its operational application in Layer 2 Spanning Tree Protocol (STP / 802.1D).

topic_title: Routing vs Forwarding, Router Architecture & Longest Prefix Match (LPM)
summary: A comprehensive deep-dive into the architectural mechanics of network layer packet delivery. Contrasts control plane routing against hardware-accelerated data plane forwarding, dissects internal router switching fabrics, details routing table structure, provides rigorous binary walkthroughs of Longest Prefix Match (LPM), and traces the hop-by-hop encapsulation lifecyle across heterogeneous network segments.
learning_objectives: Distinguish between control plane routing (calculating paths) and data plane forwarding (switching packets).
Examine physical and logical router architecture: input ports, switching fabric, output queues, and routing engines.
Interpret routing table entries: destination prefix, next hop, outgoing interface, metric, and administrative distance.
Analyze multi-router topologies interconnected via point-to-point /30 WAN links and trace connected vs remote routes.
Master the Longest Prefix Match (LPM) algorithm through bitwise binary evaluations and disambiguate overlapping subnet routes.
Configure and trace static routes, floating backup routes, and default routes (0.0.0.0/0) in Linux and enterprise routers.
Trace hop-by-hop packet forwarding: invariant IP header fields, TTL decrement, checksum recalculation, and L2 MAC frame rewrites.

topic_title: Intra-Domain and Inter-Domain Routing Protocols (RIP, OSPF, BGP)
summary: An exhaustive, rigorous masterclass on dynamic routing algorithms and protocols that power global telecommunications. Covers Distance Vector protocols and RIP convergence, the Count-to-Infinity pathology and its mathematical remedies, Link State routing and multi-area OSPF hierarchical engineering, and Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) path-vector mechanics, route selection policy hierarchies, and prefix hijacking defenses.
learning_objectives: Classify dynamic routing protocols into Interior Gateway Protocols (IGP) and Exterior Gateway Protocols (EGP).
Explain Distance Vector routing mechanics and trace distributed Bellman-Ford table updates in RIP.
Diagnose the Count-to-Infinity routing loop pathology and evaluate engineering fixes: Split Horizon, Poison Reverse, Triggered Updates, and Holddown Timers.
Analyze Link State routing and OSPF operation: Hello neighbor discovery, LSA flooding, LSDB synchronization, and Dijkstra SPF calculation.
Compute OSPF link costs using reference bandwidth formulas and design hierarchical multi-area OSPF topologies with Area 0 backbones and ABRs.

Evaluate Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) as a path-vector inter-domain protocol: Autonomous Systems (ASNs), AS-PATH loop prevention, peering vs. transit economics, and the BGP best-path decision algorithm.
Examine Internet security vulnerabilities including BGP prefix hijacking and cryptographic defenses via Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI).

topic_title: Application Layer Protocols — Domain Name System (DNS) & HTTP Architecture
summary: An exhaustive masterclass on foundational Application Layer protocols powering the modern Web. Covers the Domain Name System (DNS) distributed database and iterative resolution mechanics, URL anatomy, HTTP stateless architecture and method semantics, cryptographic cookie security and session state management, and the multi-generational transport evolution from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 multiplexing and HTTP/3 QUIC.
learning_objectives: Explain the hierarchical, decentralized architecture of the Domain Name System (DNS) from Root to TLD to Authoritative servers.
Differentiate between recursive and iterative DNS queries and trace the complete 8-stage resolution workflow.
Interpret DNS resource records (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, TXT, PTR, SOA) and execute DNS diagnostics with dig and nslookup.
Deconstruct Uniform Resource Locators (URLs) and explain why URL fragments are never transmitted over the wire.
Analyze the HTTP request/response model, evaluate HTTP methods for Safety and Idempotency, and categorize 1xx through 5xx status codes.
Implement stateful session tracking on top of stateless HTTP using secure cookies (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) and contrast cookie vs. server-side session stores.
Trace the architectural evolution of the Web from HTTP/1.0 to HTTP/1.1 (Keep-Alive, HOL blocking), HTTP/2 (binary framing, multiplexing, HPACK), and HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP).

topic_title: Transport Layer, TCP Reliability & Socket Programming
summary: An exhaustive, rigorous masterclass on the Transport Layer. Covers process-to-process addressing via 16-bit ports, contrasting lightweight UDP with the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). Deconstructs the TCP 3-way handshake, 4-way teardown, TIME_WAIT state, cumulative acknowledgment mathematics, sliding window flow control, Reno/Tahoe congestion control algorithms, socket programming implementations, and an architectural feature-by-feature comparison matrix.
learning_objectives: Explain the transport layer's role in process-to-process multiplexing and demultiplexing via port addressing.
Compare TCP and UDP architectures, header structures, and design trade-offs across real-time and reliable applications.
Trace the TCP 3-way connection establishment handshake, sequence number synchronization, and ISN randomization.
Analyze TCP 4-way termination, the half-closed state, and the engineering necessity of the 2MSL TIME_WAIT state.
Model TCP reliability mechanisms: cumulative ACKs, Round-Trip Time (RTT) estimation, Retransmission Timeouts (RTO), and Fast Retransmit via 3 duplicate ACKs.
Distinguish between Receiver Flow Control (sliding window rwnd) and Network Congestion Control (cwnd, Slow Start, AIMD).
Implement network client-server communication using low-level socket programming in Python (TCP stream and UDP datagram).
Evaluate the comprehensive feature-by-feature matrix comparing TCP and UDP across connection state, reliability, ordering, header overhead, flow control, and application selection.

summary: An exhaustive, rigorous masterclass on local network auto-configuration and edge perimeter translation. Details Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) mechanics and cache state machines, RFC 1918 private IP conservation, stateful NAT/PAT translation table lookups, DNAT port forwarding, WebRTC NAT traversal, the 4-stage DHCP DORA protocol and relay architectures, and the composite subsystems of consumer SOHO routers.
learning_objectives: Explain the operation of Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), cache lifecycle states, Gratuitous ARP, and Proxy ARP.
Categorize RFC 1918 private IPv4 address blocks and explain why they are non-routable on the public Internet.
Trace stateful Network Address Translation (NAT) and Port Address Translation (PAT / NAPT) across outbound SNAT and inbound reply flows.
Configure and evaluate Destination NAT (DNAT / Port Forwarding) and analyze NAT traversal protocols (STUN, TURN, ICE).
Trace the 4-step DHCP DORA lifecycle (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) and dissect message headers and UDP port assignments.
Calculate DHCP lease renewal timelines (T1 50% unicast, T2 87.5% broadcast, T3 100% expiry) and explain the need for DHCP Relay Agents.
Deconstruct the internal architecture of a modern SOHO home router into its six constituent subsystem components.

summary: An exhaustive, rigorous masterclass on enterprise network diagnostics and full-stack troubleshooting. Explores bottom-up OSI problem isolation, ICMP mechanics in ping and traceroute, advanced DNS debugging with dig, kernel socket inspection via ss, line-rate packet capture with tcpdump and Berkeley Packet Filters, and deep protocol analysis in Wireshark.
learning_objectives: Apply the systematic bottom-up OSI troubleshooting methodology from physical link to application layer.
Dissect ICMP mechanics in ping: Echo Request/Reply, Round-Trip Time (RTT), jitter (mdev), and Path MTU testing.
Analyze traceroute operation: intentional TTL expiration (ICMP Type 11), latency spikes, and UDP vs ICMP vs TCP probe modes.
Execute comprehensive DNS troubleshooting using dig: query sections, reverse lookups, and recursive delegation tracing via dig +trace.
Inspect active kernel socket tables and TCP connection states using ss: LISTEN, SYN_SENT, CLOSE_WAIT, and TIME_WAIT.
Capture and filter live network traffic using tcpdump with Berkeley Packet Filters (BPF) and analyze TCP flag combinations.
Analyze packet captures in Wireshark: display filters, TCP stream reassembly, and diagnosing real-world outage signatures.

topic_title: The Complete Internet Journey — From URL to Rendered Webpage
summary: The capstone masterclass of the Computer Networks curriculum. Unifies every layer, protocol, algorithm, and device into a single, cohesive chronological trace: from the instant a user types an HTTPS URL and presses Enter, through browser caching, DNS traversal, default gateway ARP resolution, TCP 3-way handshake, TLS 1.3 ECDH cryptography, 0-RTT resumption trade-offs, BGP core backbone transit, reverse proxy SSL offloading, server database query execution, response decompression, browser Critical Rendering Path DOM/CSSOM pipeline, and end-to-end troubleshooting diagnostics.
learning_objectives: Synthesize all concepts from Computer Networks into a unified, chronological 9-phase end-to-end mental model.
Trace browser cache verification, HTTP caching directives (Cache-Control, ETag), and HSTS security enforcement.
Deconstruct the complete DNS resolution sequence from browser cache to iterative root, TLD, and authoritative servers.
Analyze default gateway ARP resolution, Layer 2 frame reconstruction, and Layer 3 routing decision logic.
Examine the cryptographic TLS 1.3 handshake, Server Name Indication (SNI), X.509 certificate chains, and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key exchange mathematics.
Explain why TLS cannot replace TCP and evaluate the security vs. latency trade-offs of TLS 1.3 0-RTT session resumption.
Trace server-side infrastructure traversal: reverse proxies, SSL offloading, X-Forwarded-For headers, and database query processing.
Follow the browser Critical Rendering Path: HTML parsing, DOM tree, CSSOM tree, Render tree, Layout (reflow), and Paint.
Diagnose end-to-end failure symptoms using the unified troubleshooting map and optimize Time to First Byte (TTFB).
